title: Slab-built hexagonal tile wall panel
subtitle: Six matching hex tiles arranged in a honeycomb, grouted and mounted as a small panel
excerpt: Six hexagonal air-dry clay tiles, each 8 cm across, are cut from a single rolled slab using a card template, dried flat, then arranged in a honeycomb pattern and grouted. The finished panel hangs on a wall or sits on a worktop. No kiln needed.
sourceNotes: Hexagonal tile forms appear throughout the historical Mediterranean and Moorish tile record. Technique derived from first principles.

glossaryTerms.definition: A flat sheet of clay rolled to an even thickness, used as the building unit for tiles
Fully air-dried and unfired clay; ready for surface decoration or sealing
The drying stage at which the clay holds its shape firmly but is still slightly damp , best for refining tile edges

content.text: A hexagonal tile set uses a single rolled
slab

cut into matching hex shapes with a card template. Six tiles dried flat and arranged in a honeycomb make a panel that reads as a coherent whole. The hex shape repeats with no gaps when all six tiles are the same template size.

materials.name: PVA glue (for sealing tiles before grouting)
Small backing board (plywood or heavy card)

content.text: Cutting the template

Draw and cut a regular hexagon from card with a side length of 4 cm (total width point-to-point is 8 cm). A regular hexagon has six equal sides and six 120-degree internal angles. Measure and mark all six sides before cutting. One template cuts all six tiles.
Rolling and cutting the tiles
Roll the air-dry clay on a canvas sheet to 6 mm thickness. Use two 6 mm wooden guide rails either side of the rolling area to ensure even thickness across the slab.
Place the card template on the slab and cut around it with a fettling knife held vertically. Cut six tiles in total. Leave 2 cm of gap between each cut to avoid disturbing adjacent tiles.
Smooth the cut edges with a damp sponge while the clay is still soft, removing any knife marks.
If adding a surface impression, press a pottery stamp or lace fabric into the tile faces while still soft.
Drying the tiles flat
Flat drying is the challenge with tiles. Place each tile on a flat board. Cover loosely with a cloth for the first 24 hours to slow drying at the edges. At
leather-hard
stage, flip each tile onto a dry cloth and allow the underside to dry. Once
bone-dry
, check each tile for flatness on a flat tile or glass surface. Any tile that has warped slightly can be pressed flat under a heavy book for 24 hours before proceeding.
Sealing and grouting
Seal all tile surfaces with diluted PVA (50/50 with water). Allow to dry fully. This prevents the grout from staining the clay.
Arrange the six tiles in a honeycomb pattern on your backing board or a flat surface, with a 3 mm gap between each tile.
Mix a small amount of tile grout to a stiff paste. Work it into the gaps between tiles with a damp finger, pressing down firmly. Wipe excess grout from tile faces with a damp cloth before it sets.
Allow grout to cure for 24 hours before moving the panel.
Variations
Paint tiles with acrylic before grouting for a coloured panel.
Scale up to twelve tiles in a 3x4 arrangement for a larger backsplash panel.
Mix two different surface textures , smooth and impressed , alternating across the six tiles.
Troubleshooter

items.cause: The template shifted during cutting, or the fettling knife angled inward
items.fix: Hold the template firmly and cut with the knife blade truly vertical. Minor size differences can be sanded at bone-dry stage

items.cause: One face dried faster than the other
items.fix: Flip tiles at leather-hard to dry both sides equally. Press warped tiles under a book overnight at leather-hard before bone-dry stage

items.cause: The PVA seal was not applied, or was still wet when grouting began
items.fix: Allow the PVA coat to dry fully (at least two hours) before grouting. Stained tiles can be lightly sanded and re-sealed
